title: The boundary
hook: pilgrims enter ihram at set points around Mecca

segments.voice: Yesterday, umrah, the visit, and your line: lesser and greater. Did you get to ask anyone about their journey? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-one.

Somewhere over the desert, on the way into Jeddah, a plane full of pilgrims gets an announcement. The aircraft will soon pass the point. Up and down the aisles, people who boarded in ordinary clothes are already changed, or changing in the cramped bathrooms, or quietly saying the words that mark the start. Nothing on the ground below looks different. There's no gate, no fence, no sign you could see from the window. But the line is there, and they know it. Today, miqat.
screen: `OVER THE DESERT.` → `THE AIRCRAFT WILL SOON PASS THE POINT.` → `NO GATE, BUT A LINE.`

segments.voice: First, what a miqat is. It's a set point, a boundary place, where pilgrims heading for Mecca enter ihram, the sacred state of the pilgrimage. Before it, a person is a traveler. Past it, for Hajj or umrah, they must already be a pilgrim. Second, who set them. A hadith from Ibn Abbas in Sahih al-Bukhari names the places. Dhul Hulayfah for the people of Medina. Al-Juhfah for the people of Sham, the lands to the north. Qarn al-Manazil for the people of Najd. Yalamlam for the people of Yemen. Other reports add a point for the people of Iraq. And the hadith goes further: these points are for the people of those lands and for anyone else who passes through them on the way to Hajj or umrah. Whoever lives closer than the points enters ihram from where they are, and the people of Mecca from Mecca itself. Third, why a line at all. The places sit at different distances from Mecca, out on the roads people actually traveled. The boundary meets each traveler on their own road. Nobody walks into the sacred state by accident, and nobody slips past it unnoticed. That's why the plane announcement: scholars hold that the old points still apply in the air, so pilgrims enter ihram as they cross them, or before. Fourth, the word. Miqat also carries the sense of an appointed time. In surah seven, when Musa comes to his meeting with his Lord on the mountain, the Qur'an uses this same word for that appointed meeting. A place and a time, both set in advance, both kept. Put together, the miqat is where an ordinary journey becomes a pilgrimage. Tomorrow, what pilgrims put on once they've crossed it.
screen: `WHERE THE TRAVELER BECOMES A PILGRIM.` · `FOUR PLACES, NAMED IN BUKHARI.` · `THE LINE MEETS YOU ON YOUR ROAD.` · `A SET PLACE, AN APPOINTED TIME.`

segments.voice: The practice: think of a threshold. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a doorway you cross every day: your front door, the door to your work, the door of your car. You cross it without noticing. Now picture yourself pausing there for one breath before you step through, the way a pilgrim knows the point is coming. What would you want to leave behind on the outside? What would you want to carry in? Just notice. The bell holds the time.
Miqat. The set boundary where pilgrims to Mecca enter ihram, and a word that also carries the sense of an appointed time. Today's word.
Your line: the boundary. Today, choose one doorway and pause for a breath every time you cross it. Tomorrow: two white cloths. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Pilgrims enter ihram at or before the miqat on their route; some flying in change into ihram before boarding or on the plane, and airlines may announce when the miqat is near.

notes: Bukhari 1524 (Ibn Abbas: the four named points, and 'for those who pass through them'; Mecca's people from Mecca): confirm number.
Muslim 1183 cited for the Iraq point (Dhat Irq); confirm number and wording ('other reports add a point for the people of Iraq').
Qur'an 7:143: the Arabic li-miqatina for Musa's appointed meeting; paraphrased. Confirm.

Editor: the rule that the miqat applies to air travel is now credited to scholars, since Bukhari 1524 doesn't say it; the garbled 'cross them at the right moment' is now 'enter ihram as they cross them, or before'.
